claims.text: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state has a native, thin iron oxide layer formed under ambient conditions.
The formation and integrity of the natural iron oxide layer dictate the onset of corrosion in untreated Q235 steel.
At approximately 25°C, the passive film on untreated Q235 steel remains relatively defect-free and suppresses further corrosion.
Elevated temperature increases ionic mobility and thermal activation in the corrosion system.
Elevated temperature promotes defect formation and porosity in the passive oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Defect formation and porosity in the oxide layer accelerate corrosion initiation.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable chloride-rich environment for corrosion testing involving Q235 steel.
Comparing identically prepared Q235 samples at approximately 25°C and 60°C while holding other conditions constant isolates temperature as the intervention.
The governing structural mediator is the defect density and continuity of the passive iron oxide film.
Slower room-temperature kinetics favor a more uniform and intact oxide film.
An intact oxide film limits ion exchange and corrosion propagation.
Elevated temperature enhances chloride diffusion into the passive film.
Thermally generated pores and microcracks lower the protective capability of the film and initiate localized corrosion.
Relative to samples exposed at approximately 25°C, samples exposed at 60°C will have higher corrosion current density.
Relative to samples exposed at approximately 25°C, samples exposed at 60°C will have lower polarization resistance.
Relative to samples exposed at approximately 25°C, samples exposed at 60°C will have greater mass loss and more pronounced pitting or surface degradation.
Potentiodynamic polarization can provide corrosion current density, and polarization data can be used to calculate polarization resistance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply in chloride-rich environments up to about 60°C but may not extend to mechanically stressed or markedly different chemical environments.

Failure to observe statistically significant temperature-dependent changes in the electrochemical, mass-loss, pitting, and film-defect measurements would falsify the proposed temperature-induced film-defect mechanism.

contradictions.description: The material is described as being in a pre-exposure state in the initial-state field but as 'pre-exposed' in the boundary field.
